definition: A base model is the raw pretrained network: a text continuator with no instruction-following behavior.
details: A base model is the raw pretrained network: a text continuator with no instruction-following behavior. An instruct/chat model is the same network after post-training (SFT + preference optimization) that follows instructions, uses chat formatting, and refuses harmful requests. Confusing the two is a common deployment mistake.

explainer.lead: A language model can be good at continuing text without being good at doing what a user asks. The distinction between base and instruct models explains why, and helps prevent the wrong version from being deployed as a chat assistant.

tiers.eli5: A base model is like someone who has read lots of stories and tries to guess what words come next. An instruct model gets extra practice listening to requests, answering in a conversation, and turning down harmful ones. That is why asking the first kind to follow directions can feel confusing, while the second kind usually answers more like a helper.
tiers.practitioner: Use an instruct or chat model when an application expects instruction following, chat formatting, and refusals of harmful requests; a base model is the raw text continuator. Do not assume that the pretrained and post-trained variants are interchangeable in deployment, even when they share the same underlying network.
tiers.paperLevel: Let B denote the raw pretrained network, which performs text continuation without instruction-following behavior. Post-training produces I = PostTrain(B), using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and preference optimization, so that I follows instructions, uses chat formatting, and refuses harmful requests. The stated distinction concerns behavior added through post-training, not a different underlying network.

explainer.example: Given “Write a two-line birthday message for Ana,” a base model may simply continue the text rather than treat it as a request. After SFT and preference optimization, the instruct version responds with a two-line birthday message in chat form instead.

usedIn.name: Chat assistants
usedIn.detail: Instruct models provide instruction following, conversational formatting, and refusals of harmful requests.

usedIn.name: Text continuation
usedIn.detail: Base models serve as raw pretrained networks that continue text.

usedIn.name: Model deployment
usedIn.detail: Teams must distinguish the variants to avoid shipping a text continuator where a chat model is expected.

explainer.intuition: Pretraining produces a network that continues text; it does not by itself produce instruction-following behavior. Post-training turns that same network into an instruct or chat model with conversational behavior.
howItWorks: Start with the raw pretrained network, called the base model.
Treat its behavior as text continuation rather than instruction following.
Apply post-training with supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization.
The resulting instruct model follows instructions and uses chat formatting.
It also refuses harmful requests, making its deployment behavior different from the base model's.
explainer.whyItMatters: Choosing the wrong variant can produce a deployment that continues text when users expect helpful, formatted answers. Recognizing that the instruct model is a post-trained version of the same network clarifies both its capabilities and its origin.
misconceptions: A base model is not an instruction-following chat assistant; it is a text continuator.
An instruct model is not necessarily a different underlying network; it can be the same network after post-training.
The two variants are not interchangeable in deployment, because their behavior differs.
